questions.q: The symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$ acts on $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ by permuting variables. Which classical result identifies the invariant subring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\mathfrak{S}_n}$?
choices: It is generated as a $k$-algebra by the elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, which are algebraically independent.
It coincides with the original ring.
questions.explain: The fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials says every symmetric polynomial is uniquely a polynomial in $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ (or equivalently the power sums $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ in characteristic zero), and these $n$ generators are algebraically independent. So $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\mathfrak{S}_n}\cong k[e_1,\ldots,e_n]$, a polynomial ring on $n$ variables — the cleanest possible finite generation.

questions.q: The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n$ acts on $k[x]$ by $x\mapsto\zeta x$ for a primitive $n$-th root of unity $\zeta$ (assume $\operatorname{char}k\nmid n$). How many algebra generators does the invariant ring $k[x]^{\mathbb{Z}/n}$ require?
questions.explain: Only the monomials $x^{kn}$ are fixed (other monomials $x^m$ get multiplied by $\zeta^m\ne 1$). So $k[x]^{\mathbb{Z}/n}=k[x^n]$, generated by the single element $x^n$. The Reynolds operator $R(f)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_k \zeta^{-k\deg}\cdot f$ projects onto this subring.

questions.q: Hilbert's 1890 finiteness theorem (the engine of classical invariant theory) asserts that the invariant ring $R^G$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra provided:
choices: $G$ is any algebraic group at all.
questions.explain: Finite generation of $R^G$ holds for reductive $G$ acting linearly on $R$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. For finite groups (which are reductive in characteristic zero, and even more generally when $\operatorname{char}k\nmid|G|$), it's a much older theorem of Noether. Nagata constructed a unipotent counterexample in 1959 — a 14-dimensional unipotent group acting on $k[x_1,\ldots,x_{32}]$ with non-finitely-generated invariants — disproving Hilbert's 14th problem in general.

questions.q: Select every algebraic group that is reductive over $\mathbb{C}$.
choices: The unipotent group $U_n$ of upper-triangular matrices with $1$s on the diagonal
questions.explain: $\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\mathrm{SL}_n$, and tori are reductive — they have trivial unipotent radical and every finite-dimensional representation is semisimple in characteristic zero. $\mathbb{G}_a$ and unipotent groups are not reductive: their representations have nontrivial extensions (e.g.\ $\mathbb{G}_a$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$ as $t\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has no invariant complement to the $x$-axis).

questions.q: The Reynolds operator $R\colon V\to V^G$ for a reductive $G$ is characterised by:
choices: A $G$-equivariant projection onto $V^G$ that splits the inclusion $V^G\hookrightarrow V$.
An arbitrary linear map fixing constants.
A non-commutative operator that fails to commute with the action.
questions.explain: Reductivity (= every $G$-rep is semisimple) gives a canonical $G$-equivariant projection $R\colon V\twoheadrightarrow V^G$ with $R|_{V^G}=\mathrm{id}$. Over a compact group it is the Haar-average $R(v)=\int_K k\cdot v\,dk$; for algebraic reductive groups it is the analogous algebraic averaging. Without $R$ there is no way to take "the invariant part" of an arbitrary section, and Hilbert's finiteness proof breaks.

questions.q: Nagata (1959) constructed a unipotent group action whose invariant ring is not finitely generated. Which question of Hilbert did this resolve?
choices: Hilbert's 14th problem (finite generation of invariant rings).
questions.explain: Hilbert's 14th problem asked whether $R^G$ is always finitely generated for an algebraic group $G$ acting on a polynomial ring $R$. Nagata's counterexample (a 14-dimensional unipotent group acting on a polynomial ring in 32 variables) showed the answer is no in general — but yes for reductive $G$, which is what makes reductivity the right hypothesis for GIT.

questions.q: Match each stability class of a linearized $G$-action on $X$ to its defining property.
right: Orbit closed in the semistable locus, finite stabilizer
Orbit closed in the semistable locus, possibly positive-dimensional stabilizer
Some $G$-invariant section is nonzero on $x$, but $\overline{G\cdot x}$ meets a strictly smaller orbit
No nonzero $G$-invariant section misses $x$ (every $G$-invariant section vanishes there)
questions.explain: Unstable = every invariant section vanishes; semistable = some invariant section is nonzero (the points that survive the quotient); strictly semistable = semistable but the orbit closure absorbs smaller orbits, so several orbits collapse to one quotient point; stable = closed orbit with finite stabilizer (so the orbit is a single quotient point and has the right dimension); polystable = closed orbit but the stabilizer may be larger (the orbit still represents a unique quotient point but isn't "generic").

questions.q: Let $X$ be projective with a linearized $G$-action ($G$ reductive). The GIT quotient $X/\!/_L G$ is constructed as:
choices: The topological orbit space $X/G$ with the quotient topology.
questions.explain: The graded ring of invariant sections of all powers of $L$ is the input to Proj — that's how the projective GIT quotient inherits an ample line bundle from $L$. The affine case (the original Hilbert quotient) is the special case $X=\operatorname{Spec} R$, $X/\!/G=\operatorname{Spec} R^G$. The topological orbit space is too coarse — non-closed orbits in the semistable locus get identified into a single quotient point, which the topology can't see.

questions.q: Consider $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ acting on $(\mathbb{P}^1)^n$ by the diagonal Möbius action. A configuration $(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$ is GIT-unstable iff:
choices: Some single point appears with multiplicity strictly greater than $n/2$ (i.e.\ a strict majority of the points coincide).
questions.explain: For $(\mathbb{P}^1)^n$ under $\mathrm{SL}_2$ with the symmetric linearization, the Hilbert–Mumford criterion says $(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$ is semistable iff no point appears more than $n/2$ times, stable iff no point appears $\ge n/2$ times. So unstable = strict majority coincide (a 1-PS fixing the majority point drives the whole configuration to it). The classic baby example is $n=4$: four distinct points are stable (their cross-ratio is the quotient $M_{0,4}\cong\mathbb{P}^1$), three coinciding is unstable.

questions.q: Let $\lambda\colon\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathrm{SL}_2$ be the 1-PS $\lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$ acting on a binary form $f(x,y)=\sum a_i x^i y^{n-i}$. Under $\lambda$, the monomial $x^i y^{n-i}$ has weight:
questions.explain: Under $\lambda(t)\cdot(x,y)=(tx,t^{-1}y)$, the monomial $x^i y^{n-i}$ becomes $t^{i}\cdot t^{-(n-i)}\cdot x^i y^{n-i}=t^{2i-n}\cdot x^i y^{n-i}$. So weight $2i-n$: negative for $i<n/2$, zero at $i=n/2$, positive for $i>n/2$. The Hilbert–Mumford weight $\mu(f,\lambda)=\min\{2i-n:a_i\ne 0\}$.

questions.q: For the binary quartic $f(x,y)=x^3 y$ (so $n=4$ and only the $i=3$ coefficient is nonzero) and $\lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$, compute the Hilbert–Mumford weight $\mu(f,\lambda)$.
questions.explain: Only the $i=3$ coefficient is nonzero, contributing weight $2\cdot 3-4=2$. Since $\mu>0$, this 1-PS drives $f$ away from $0$ (so $f$ is in fact semistable for this $\lambda$ — only $\lambda^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(t^{-1},t)$ would push $f\to 0$, with weight $-2$). The Hilbert–Mumford criterion looks at the worst 1-PS: $f=x^3y$ has minimum weight $-2$ over all conjugate 1-PSs (just swap which axis is shrunk), and so $f$ is unstable for $\mathrm{SL}_2$ — a triple root is too much.

questions.q: Order the steps in applying the Hilbert–Mumford criterion to test whether $x\in X$ is semistable for a $G$-action linearized in $L$.
items: For each 1-PS, compute $\mu(x,\lambda)$ as the minimum weight $w$ over weight components $x_w\neq 0$.
Enumerate (or parametrise) the 1-parameter subgroups $\lambda\colon\mathbb{G}_m\to G$ up to conjugacy.
Decompose the action of $\lambda$ on the ambient $V=H^0(X,L)$ into weight spaces $V=\bigoplus V_w$, and write $x=\sum x_w$.
Declare $x$ semistable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)\le 0$ for every $\lambda$; stable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)<0$ for every nontrivial $\lambda$.
questions.explain: Standard workflow: parametrise 1-PSs (often it suffices to test only finitely many up to conjugacy, like the diagonal ones for $\mathrm{SL}_n$), decompose the ambient representation under each $\lambda$ into weight pieces, read off the minimum weight where $x$ has nonzero support, then apply the $\le 0$ / $<0$ test. The pedagogical example is $\mathrm{SL}_2$ on binary $n$-forms: diagonal 1-PSs give the weight $2i-n$ on $x^iy^{n-i}$, and the criterion becomes "no root has multiplicity $>n/2$."

questions.q: The Kempf–Ness theorem (1979) identifies a GIT quotient with a symplectic reduction. Which equality does it establish?
choices: $X/\!/_L G_\mathbb{C}\;\cong\;\mu^{-1}(0)/K$, where $\mu\colon X\to\mathfrak{k}^*$ is a moment map and $K$ is a maximal compact in $G_\mathbb{C}$.
Every GIT quotient is symplectic but not Kähler.
questions.explain: Kempf–Ness is the bridge: the projective GIT quotient $X/\!/_L G_\mathbb{C}$ (algebraic) coincides with the Marsden–Weinstein reduction $\mu^{-1}(0)/K$ (symplectic). Moreover, a $G_\mathbb{C}$-orbit is polystable iff it intersects $\mu^{-1}(0)$, and in that case the intersection is a single $K$-orbit. So stability is the algebraic shadow of "the moment map can be solved".

questions.q: Under Kempf–Ness, an orbit $G_\mathbb{C}\cdot x$ that contains a zero of the moment map $\mu$ is necessarily:
questions.explain: If $\mu(x)=0$ for some $x$ in the orbit, the orbit through that point is closed (the moment-map norm-square $\|\mu\|^2$ is a Morse–Bott function whose only critical orbits along the gradient flow are closed orbits at level zero). Closed orbit in the semistable locus = polystable. Conversely, every polystable orbit contains a zero of $\mu$, and that zero is unique up to the action of the maximal compact $K$.

questions.q: Which of the following are direct consequences of the Kempf–Ness theorem?
choices: The GIT quotient inherits a Kähler structure from the symplectic reduction (when one starts from a Kähler $X$).
Stability can be tested by minimising the moment-map norm-square $\|\mu\|^2$ along $G_\mathbb{C}$-orbits.
Every reductive $G$ is a maximal compact $K$ (false in general).
Moduli problems with a symplectic interpretation (stable bundles, ASD connections) admit an algebraic incarnation as a GIT quotient.
questions.explain: Kempf–Ness directly gives the Kähler quotient (the symplectic reduction inherits a complex structure from the GIT side and a metric from the symplectic side), supplies the minimisation algorithm for stability ($\|\mu\|^2$-flow lands at the polystable orbit), and identifies moduli of stable bundles / instantons (Atiyah–Bott, Donaldson) with GIT quotients. The claim that $G=K$ is false — $K$ is a proper subgroup of $G_\mathbb{C}$ (real form vs complexification).

questions.q: In variation of GIT (VGIT), the parameter being varied is:
questions.explain: VGIT fixes $G$ and $X$ but varies the linearized polarization $L$. Different chambers in the $G$-ample cone (the cone of $G$-linearized $\mathbb{Q}$-line bundles where $X^{ss}(L)$ is non-empty) give different semistable loci and hence different quotients $X/\!/_L G$. Walls separate these chambers.

questions.q: Crossing a wall in VGIT typically changes the GIT quotient by:
choices: A small birational modification (often a flip in the MMP sense).
An isomorphism — quotients on opposite sides of a wall are always equal.
questions.explain: Thaddeus / Dolgachev–Hu (1998): crossing a wall in VGIT replaces $X/\!/_{L_+} G$ by $X/\!/_{L_-} G$ via a small modification — a flip if both quotients are projective with isomorphic codimension-$\ge 2$ open subsets, sometimes a divisorial contraction or a blow-up. The wall itself parametrises a strictly-semistable locus that is contracted from both sides. This is one of the cleanest natural settings in which the MMP runs explicitly.

questions.q: Which of the following moduli problems is not a standard application of VGIT?
choices: Moduli of pointed curves $\overline{M}_{g,n}$ as $n$ varies.
Moduli of vector bundles on a curve as the stability slope varies.
Bridgeland stability conditions on $D^b(X)$ — wall and chamber structure on $\mathrm{Stab}(X)$.
Frobenius eigenvalues of $\ell$-adic sheaves under Galois action.
questions.explain: Bridgeland's stability conditions on derived categories are the modern heir of VGIT — they organise moduli problems by a continuous parameter with walls. Slope stability of vector bundles and moduli of pointed curves also fit. Frobenius eigenvalues of $\ell$-adic sheaves are a number-theoretic / étale phenomenon (Weil II / Deligne) with no GIT-style wall-crossing in the sense of the others.

questions.q: Match each moduli problem to the GIT construction that produces it.
left: Moduli of representations of a quiver $Q$ with dimension vector $\mathbf{d}$ and stability character $\theta$
Moduli of semistable vector bundles on a smooth projective curve
right: $X^{ss}(\theta)/\!/_\theta\mathrm{GL}(\mathbf{d})$ where $X$ is the representation space and $\theta$-stability matches GIT stability (King)
Mumford's GIT on Hilbert points of pluri-canonically embedded curves
Period domain quotients (a Hodge-theoretic, not direct-GIT, construction)
Geometric invariant theory of semistable bundles via Quot schemes (Seshadri / Gieseker)
questions.explain: Mumford's $M_g$: tricanonical Hilbert points are stable iff the curve is Deligne–Mumford stable; the quotient is $M_g$. King: quiver representations have a GIT-natural character that matches slope stability. Seshadri–Gieseker: semistable bundles on a curve correspond to Quot-scheme points stable under $\mathrm{GL}$. Polarized K3 moduli: the natural construction is via Hodge structures and period maps, not directly GIT — although GIT plays a role in compactifications and the Hilbert-point picture.

questions.q: King's theorem on quiver moduli identifies $\theta$-stability with GIT stability for $\mathrm{GL}(\mathbf{d})=\prod_i\mathrm{GL}(d_i)$ acting on $\mathrm{Rep}(Q,\mathbf{d})$. The character $\theta\in\mathbb{Z}^{Q_0}$ enters the picture as:
choices: The linearization of the trivial bundle by the character $\theta\colon\mathrm{GL}(\mathbf{d})\to\mathbb{G}_m$.
An extra group element commuting with $\mathrm{GL}(\mathbf{d})$.
An étale cover of the representation space.
questions.explain: King's construction: $\theta$ is a tuple $(\theta_i)\in\mathbb{Z}^{Q_0}$ with $\sum_i\theta_i d_i=0$; it determines a character of $\prod\mathrm{GL}(d_i)$ by $g\mapsto\prod\det(g_i)^{\theta_i}$ which linearizes the trivial line bundle on the representation space. A representation is $\theta$-semistable iff it is GIT-semistable for that linearization. Varying $\theta$ runs VGIT on quiver moduli — wall-crossing produces the elementary equivalences of derived categories of quiver representations.

questions.q: Why is GIT (rather than just taking the orbit space $X/G$ as a topological quotient) needed to construct $M_g$ as a separated scheme?
choices: $X/G$ is generally non-Hausdorff because non-closed orbits in the semistable locus collapse to the same point — GIT instead identifies them, producing a separated scheme.
$G$ does not act on the Hilbert scheme.
$M_g$ is not separated even with GIT.
questions.explain: The naive orbit space is non-separated whenever the action has non-closed orbits — exactly what happens in moduli problems with a positive-dimensional stabiliser or with limits across the unstable locus. GIT's coarse quotient identifies orbits with non-disjoint closures, exactly enough to make the quotient separated. This is also why $\overline{M}_g$ (Deligne–Mumford) is the right compactification — it absorbs the strictly semistable locus into nodal curves with finite automorphism.
